title: A Land Swap Stirs Debate on Wild Cumberland Island
summary:
Wild horses, feral hogs, and deer roam free on Cumberland Island, Georgia, an 18-mile barrier island off the Atlantic coast. Its salt marshes, maritime forests, and untouched beach, reachable only by ferry, make it among the most ecologically diverse islands on the coast. The National Park Service has managed it since 1972, including about 9,800 acres of wilderness Congress said 'shall be permanently preserved in its primitive state.'

But the island holds more than wilderness: relics, mission remnants, plantation ruins, and grand homes built by Gilded Age industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy. Carnegie descendants still live or vacation here on private land, and the park service has proposed a land swap with them, allowing new construction.

Under the proposal, parkland on the island's west side would go to two branches of Carnegie descendants for up to eight new private homes. Park superintendent Melissa Trenchik says gathering private ownership on the west side would let the park better protect natural and cultural sites on the Atlantic side, where development could then be banned.

Trenchik calls the eight homes 'modest,' saying they would face permanent conservation limits. Critics disagree, noting the 15,000-square-foot allowance, including driveway and outbuildings. 'We're swapping for McMansions,' said Joseph Manning, an attorney with Defenders of Wildlife.

Barclay McFadden, a descendant of Thomas Carnegie, calls the fears about mansions 'so unfounded.' 'Five generations have been buried there,' he said. 'For our children and our grandchildren, it's a sacred place.' He says his family has been 'wonderful stewards of the island.'

Naturalist Carol Ruckdeschel, 85, has lived on the island for more than 50 years and is one of the main voices against the swap. She worries it is the 'first nose under the tent' toward more development, and says the island should stay a pure wilderness.
why_it_matters: Cumberland Island is one of the most ecologically diverse islands on the coast, so the choice between new homes and keeping it wild will shape what this rare place looks like for future visitors and wildlife.

background_read: A national park is a large area of land that a country protects so its nature and history can stay safe for everyone to enjoy.
Barrier islands are long, narrow islands off the coast that protect the mainland from storms and waves, and their marshes and forests are home to many kinds of wildlife.
Sometimes private land sits inside or beside a national park, and the park service may trade land with the owners to bring the park's most important places under its care.
When a trade like this is suggested, people often disagree about whether new building will harm the wild land or help protect it.
